content: 1. The effectiveness of a soybean-maize-sorghum-based ready-to-use complementary food paste on infant growth was studied in South Kivu, Democratic Republic of Congo, and published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2012. 2. Blood retinol concentrations in infants fed complementary foods fortified with Moringa Oleifera leaf powder were measured in a pilot study, as reported in the Annals of Nutrition & Metabolism in 2017. 3. A pilot study demonstrated that complementary foods fortified with Moringa Oleifera leaf powder improved blood retinol concentrations in infants, as published in the Yale Journal of Biology and Medicine in 2018. 4. The impact of complementary foods fortified with Moringa Oleifera leaf powder on hemoglobin concentration and infant growth in Ghana's Eastern Region was explored in a study published in Food Science in 2019. 5. A study from 1987 examined the long-term consumption of beef extended with soy protein and its effects on iron status in men, women, and children, as published in Plant Foods for Human Nutrition. 6. The efficacy of a locally-produced, multiple micronutrient-fortified ready-to-use supplementary food (RUSF) for children under two years in Cambodia was evaluated and published in the Annals of Nutrition & Metabolism in 2017. 7. A randomized controlled trial tested the effectiveness of a locally-produced RUSF in preventing growth faltering and improving micronutrient status in children under two years in Cambodia, as described in Nutrition Journal in 2018. 8. The acceptability of locally-produced RUSF for children under two years in Cambodia was assessed in a cluster randomized trial, with findings published in Maternal & Child Nutrition in 2019. 9. A randomized controlled trial conducted by Boston University in 2008 tested the effects of a multi-nutrient fortified juice on health outcomes. 10. A double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled intervention trial in Morocco demonstrated that iron fortification using NaFeEDTA reduced lead burden and improved iron status in lead-exposed children, as reported in 2015. 11. A cross-sectional study and randomized trial investigated the relationship between vitamin D status and immune health outcomes in healthy young children, as published in Nutrients in 2018. 12. The effect of phytase on zinc absorption from millet-based porridge in young Burkinabe children was studied and published in the European Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2017. 13. A study compared the effects of zinc delivered in fortified food versus a liquid supplement on growth, morbidity, and plasma zinc concentrations in young Peruvian children, as published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2007. 14. Children receiving complementary food supplements in rural Bangladesh had higher nutrient intakes from home foods, as reported in the FASEB Journal in 2015. 15. An enteropathy score was found to predict subsequent growth better than the lactulose-mannitol ratio in children enrolled in a community-based randomized trial of complementary food supplements in rural Bangladesh, as published in the FASEB Journal in 2016. 16. The effect of complementary food supplementation on breastfeeding and home diet in rural Bangladeshi children was studied and published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2016. 17. Biomarkers of environmental enteric dysfunction among children in rural Bangladesh were examined in a study published in the Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition in 2017. 18. Complementary food supplements were shown to increase dietary nutrient adequacy without replacing home food consumption in children aged 6-18 months in rural Bangladesh, as reported in the Journal of Nutrition in 2018. 19. Micronutrient and inflammation status following one year of complementary food supplementation in 18-month-old rural Bangladeshi children was evaluated in a randomized controlled trial, as published in Nutrients in 2020. 20. The effects of iron supplementation on hematological and anthropometric parameters in the first two years of life were studied, highlighting risks and benefits, as published in Hematology in 2011. 21. Iron-fortified lentils were tested as a strategy to improve iron status in Bangladeshi children in a study conducted in 2019. 22. Iron bioavailability from lipid-based complementary food fortificants mixed with millet porridge was optimized by adding phytase and ascorbic acid, as reported in the Journal of Nutrition in 2013. 23. A study in Thailand evaluated iron bioavailability in children aged 8-24 months from micronutrient-fortified quick-cooking rice containing ferric ammonium citrate or a mixture of ferrous sulfate and ferric sodium EDTA, as published in Maternal & Child Nutrition in 2015. 24. Micronutrient fortification was tested to improve growth and health outcomes in maternally HIV-exposed and unexposed Zambian infants in a randomized controlled trial, as published in PLoS ONE in 2010. 25. Determinants of infant feeding choices by Zambian mothers were explored in a mixed-methods study published in Maternal & Child Nutrition in 2011. 26. Zinc absorption from biofortified maize was found to meet the requirements of young rural Zambian children, as reported in the Journal of Nutrition in 2015. 27. An intervention study in a Bangladeshi slum showed suboptimal growth among children receiving a food supplement for five months, as published in Acta Paediatrica in 2016. 28. The effect of fortified complementary food supplementation on child growth in rural Bangladesh was evaluated in a cluster-randomized trial, as reported in the FASEB Journal in 2015. 29. A study in Burkina Faso compared four supplementary foods for preventing stunting and wasting among children aged 6-23 months, as described in the FASEB Journal in 2017. 30. The cost-effectiveness of four specialized nutritious foods in preventing stunting and wasting in children aged 6-23 months in Burkina Faso was evaluated in a geographically randomized trial, as published in 2020. 31. The influence of different cereal grains on iron absorption from infant cereal foods was studied and published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 1997. 32. An infant feeding intervention for HIV-exposed Haitian infants was evaluated in a study conducted in 2010. 33. A feeding trial of biofortified pearl millet was conducted in 2012. 34. A study assessed the effectiveness of ready-to-use therapeutic food in treating uncomplicated severe acute malnutrition in under-five children in community settings, as registered in 2011. 35. The impact of iron-rich baby food on increasing blood iron levels and reducing the risk of iron deficiency was evaluated in 2017. 36. The Dharavi Nutrition Project was conducted to assess nutritional interventions, as registered in 2017. 37. The inclusion of cereals enriched with tryptophan, adenosine-5'-phosphate, and uridine-5'-phosphate at supper was shown to improve infant sleep quality, as published in Nutrition Neuroscience in 2009. 38. The acceptability and home use of a ready-to-consume complementary food in rural Guatemala were evaluated in 2016. 39. The Society for Nutrition Education and Behavior's 52nd Annual Conference in 2019 discussed nutrition education rooted in food, as reported in the Journal of Nutrition Education and Behavior. 40. A baby-led approach to complementary feeding was shown to impact iron intake and status at 12 months of age in a randomized controlled trial, as published in the European Journal of Pediatrics in 2016. 41. The impact of a baby-led approach to complementary feeding on iron status at 12 months of age was further explored in a study published in Nutrients in 2017. 42. Iron bioavailability in infants from cereal fortified with ferric pyrophosphate or ferrous fumarate was studied and published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2000. 43. The addition of retinyl palmitate to iron-fortified maize porridge improved erythrocyte iron incorporation in African children with vitamin A deficiency, as reported in the British Journal of Nutrition in 2003. 44. Iron-fortified orange juice was used to control iron-deficiency anemia in Brazilian preschool children, as published in Nutrition Research in 2003. 45. Drinking water fortified with iron and ascorbic acid was tested as a strategy to control anemia in Brazilian preschool children, as reported in Food and Nutrition Bulletin in 2005. 46. Drinking water fortified with iron and ascorbic acid was further assessed in daycare centers as a strategy to control iron-deficiency anemia, as published in the Journal of Tropical Pediatrics in 2014. 47. New formulations for fortified-blended foods were tested in the MFFAPP Tanzania efficacy trial, as reported in the FASEB Journal in 2017. 48. The MFFAPP Tanzania efficacy study protocol evaluated newly formulated, extruded, fortified blended foods for food aid, as published in 2017. 49. Complementary feeding of sorghum-based and corn-based fortified blended foods resulted in similar iron, vitamin A, and anthropometric outcomes in the MFFAPP Tanzania efficacy study, as reported in 2019. 50. The impact of a dietary supplement on the nutritional status of preschool children in daycare centers was evaluated in a study published in Revista de Nutrição in 2006. 51. Iron fortification of domestic drinking water was tested as a strategy to prevent anemia among low socioeconomic families in Brazil, as published in the International Journal of Food Science and Nutrition in 1996. 52. The use of sugar fortified with iron tris-glycinate chelate was evaluated for preventing iron-deficiency anemia in preschool children, as published in Archivos Latinoamericanos de Nutrición in 2001. 53. Cytokine response to dietary rehabilitation with curd (Indian dahi) and leaf protein concentrate in malnourished children was studied and published in the Indian Journal of Medical Research in 2009. 54. The effects of the age of introduction of complementary foods on the iron status of breastfed infants in Honduras were studied and published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 1998. 55. Exclusive breastfeeding for six months, with iron supplementation, was shown to maintain adequate micronutrient status among term, low-birthweight, breastfed infants in Honduras, as published in the Journal of Nutrition in 2004. 56. The mode of delivery of iron or iron and zinc on iron status and iron stress markers was evaluated in a study published in Archives of Disease in Childhood in 2012. 57. The effectiveness of complementary food supplements in improving the nutritional status of elder infants and young children in areas affected by the Wenchuan earthquake was studied and published in PLoS ONE in 2013. 58. The effectiveness of locally-produced peanut/milk spread and newly developed ready-to-use foods (RUF) for malnourished children in Nias Island, Indonesia, was evaluated in 2014. 59. Complementary food with low (8%) or high (12%) meat content as a source of dietary iron was tested in a double-blinded randomized controlled trial, as published in the European Journal of Nutrition in 2010. 60. Oligofructose-supplemented infant cereal was tested in two randomized, blinded, community-based trials in Peruvian infants, as published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2003. 61. An acceptability trial of desiccated beef liver and meat powder as potential fortifiers of complementary diets for young children in Indonesia was conducted and published in the Journal of Food Science in 2017. 62. Drinking water as an iron carrier to control anemia in preschool children in daycare centers was evaluated in a study published in 2014.
